Dear Marc,

Thanks so much, the model runs without any problems now. I had my data array and covariates in the right format, but I had assumed that I should use NAs for the covariates where surveys were missing. I replaced the NAs with 0s. So I understand correctly, does the actual value for the missing surveys not matter? If the observation array has NA, does JAGS skip that site x replicate x species combination, it's just that the covariate datasets cannot have NA's in them?

Thanks again,
Tom

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tom,

a short and, naturally not 100% correct, “formula” for how to deal with NAs in JAGS and Nimble (and WinBUGS) is: NAs in the response, no problem, NAs in explanatory variables: have to be dealt with.

Meaning: missing responses are informed by the model and the data, but missing covariates are not. In your case, where you created the same NA pattern in response and covariates just to induce balance and therefore simpler and neater JAGS code, filling up the missing covariates with any admissible numerical value will work, as long as there is never any non-missing value at the corresponding position in the response. Thus, these filled-in covariates are innocuous, since they will not contribute to the likelihood. If, however, you have missing covariates in positions were there is a non-missing response, then just filling in any value is not right and the traditional rules for formal missing value imputations come into play: ideally, then, you specify a model for the missing covariate values (which in the simplest case may for instance just be a Normal with mean and variance that are estimated from the non-missing covariates).

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Model with data augmentation
messages.body_plain:
Dear team,
I hope this email finds you well.
I have been using a multi-state model to estimate population sizes and transition probabilities as presented in the BPA book.
I am working on a simulated population, right now and I am having quite an interesting behavior in my model.
I have run the model several times (more than 50) to check how reliable are the estimates and half of the time the model wants to use all the data augmentation given to it, so the first or second estimates or population size are considerable high (almost the size of the date set with the augmented data) and then it suddenly gets super close to the simulated sample size. sometimes it stats well and the jump is in the middle or at the end.
has someone experienced similar behavior? if so, how is it possible to handle it?

Thank you in advance :)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Diego,

perhaps that scale prior of Link may be useful for you. When doing data augmentation, you augment the detection histories with all-zero histories and then add another hierarchical level to your model which decides whether an individual is 'real' or not. This model for the data augmentation variables is a Bernoulli with some success probability, omega say. The usual choice for a prior for omega is a uniform, which is then equivalent to putting a discrete uniform prior on population size N. However, Link shows that this choice sometimes makes the estimate of N to "run away", and that this can be prevented by that scale prior.

Not completely sure this is the solution, but I just wanted to follow up.

best regards  -- Marc

# Likelihood

Hello all,
Thank you for the help and ideas that are coming from all sides.
The model that I am trying to implement is an extension of the one in page 342 of the BPA book, JS model as a multistate model.

In this case, the population size es calculated as:

          for(i in 1:M){

          for(t in 2:n.occasions){

                    al[i, t-1]<-equals(z[i,t], 2)

           }

           }

     for(i in 1:n.occasions){

          N[t] <- sum( al[, t]) # Actual population size

      }

This the what is happening to the results of the MCMC. the evolution of the population size looks as:

Top panel: time in the x-axis and number of individuals in the y-axis, the black line is the posterior mean of the 3 chains, red line is the posterior median, green dotted lines present the credible intervals

Bottom panel: time in the x-axis and number of individuals on the y-axis, solid line posterior mean with credible interval on the dotted line, each chain is a different color

blue dots represent the true simulated population size, on both samples.

It is interesting to me why there is a sudden jump in time 9, just for one chain.

Also when the jump is not in the middle, it is clearly shown at the begging of the trend, 1st and second-time points.

I related this problem to the parameters of the observation matrix (observation process). If I run the model with values of the matrix as a constant for all the parameters the result is deal, there is no sudden jump.

 The values of the observation matrix present the following results at times 10 and 11

The left (right) panel presents the posterior mean for the observation parameter at time 10(11), each chain is a different color

I have been trying to give different distributions to this parameter. and the results are still similar. right now I am trying a truncated beta(10, 10)

but I don't expect to solve the issue, just to make it less frequent.

all the models are run in NIMBLE and I am also blocking some parameters to improve sampling.

any ideas?

Thank you all for your time :)

messages.subject: Advice on using count data with uncertainty as census data in IPMs (JAGS)
messages.subject_clean: Advice on using count data with uncertainty as census data in IPMs (JAGS)
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I am doing some test IPMs to see how I can use different data sources of my study population. An interesting approach would be to use count data with associated uncertainty as census data in my IPM. Generally, count data is implemented as C[t] ~ dnorm(N[t], tau), where C is the count data, N is the estimated population size of the model, and tau is the precision estimate. In most IPMs, C is obtained from censuses or surveys and there is only one single measure per year without any associated uncertainty. In my case, I am thinking of estimating C using a model of population size. I have seen that this approach was used before, so it should be possible (see Tempel, Peery, & Gutiérrez, 2014 studying California spotted owls and incorporating population size estimates from an occupancy model as count data).

I have two potential approaches to address this, but both raise questions I do not know how to address so far.

1) Ideally, I would like to create a submodel inside my IPM to estimate population size by year. The big issue here is that my estimate of population counts C must be defined at the left side of either a stochastic or a deterministic relationship. E.g.: C[t] <- sum(x[1:10]). Then, whenever I define the stochastic relationship between my estimate of count data and the population size estimate by my IPM's population dynamics process, I must define count data again at the left of the relationship: C[t] ~ dnorm(N[t], tau). To my knowledge, defining C both times at the left side of a relationship should lead to a fatal error as I am defining a variable twice.

2)  Another choice is to create a model to estimate population counts, and then incorporate the result as data for my IPM. The issue here is that my population count results will be formatted as a matrix (years * iterations). At the time of incorporating these data to the IPM, if I incorporated only the means of my results, I would be ignoring all uncertainty associated. If I extracted the mean and sd of every year's count, I would not know how to incorporate both values in the stochastic relationship between counts and population size C[t] ~ dnorm(N[t], tau).

Has anybody here been through this, or know an optimal solution to this situation?

Thank you in advance, have a nice day!

Jaume

Hi Jaume,

The first approach is indeed not possible (or at least I do not know how to resolve the problem that you pointed out). However, the second approach that you sketched out is a possible way. Let's assume that you have estimates of annual abundance (i[t]) and an associated SE (SE(I[t])) from your population data. Then there are 2 ways to proceed.
you assume that the errors in the estimated abundance is the same as the errors in the IPM. Then you would use as the observation model in the IPM: i[t] ~ Normal(N[t], SD(i[t])), where N[t] is the population size in the IPM.
you assume that there is additional error in the IPM, e.g. because of lack of fit in other parts of the IPM (more realistic in my opinion). To accomodate additional error, you first 'estimate' a population index as i[t] ~ Normal(y[t], SD(i[t])), and then relate it with the IPM population size as y[t] ~ Normal(N[t], sigma). Sigma is a parameter for which you give a prior and represents the additional error/uncertainty.
You can find descriptions of option 1 in Robinson et al. (2014, 10.1111/2041-210X.12204), and of option 2 in Fay et al. (2019, doi: 10.1111/ecog.04559) and in our IPM book chapter 6.6.4.

Kind regards

Michael

> Betreff: Advice on using count data with uncertainty as census data in IPMs (JAGS)
>
> Hi all!
>
> I am doing some test IPMs to see how I can use different data sources of my study population. An interesting approach would be to use count data with associated uncertainty as census data in my IPM. Generally, count data is implemented as C[t] ~ dnorm(N[t], tau), where C is the count data, N is the estimated population size of the model, and tau is the precision estimate. In most IPMs, C is obtained from censuses or surveys and there is only one single measure per year without any associated uncertainty. In my case, I am thinking of estimating C using a model of population size. I have seen that this approach was used before, so it should be possible (see Tempel, Peery, & Gutiérrez, 2014 studying California spotted owls and incorporating population size estimates from an occupancy model as count data).
>
> I have two potential approaches to address this, but both raise questions I do not know how to address so far.
>
> 1) Ideally, I would like to create a submodel inside my IPM to estimate population size by year. The big issue here is that my estimate of population counts C must be defined at the left side of either a stochastic or a deterministic relationship. E.g.: C[t] <- sum(x[1:10]). Then, whenever I define the stochastic relationship between my estimate of count data and the population size estimate by my IPM's population dynamics process, I must define count data again at the left of the relationship: C[t] ~ dnorm(N[t], tau). To my knowledge, defining C both times at the left side of a relationship should lead to a fatal error as I am defining a variable twice.
>
> 2)  Another choice is to create a model to estimate population counts, and then incorporate the result as data for my IPM. The issue here is that my population count results will be formatted as a matrix (years * iterations). At the time of incorporating these data to the IPM, if I incorporated only the means of my results, I would be ignoring all uncertainty associated. If I extracted the mean and sd of every year's count, I would not know how to incorporate both values in the stochastic relationship between counts and population size C[t] ~ dnorm(N[t], tau).
>
> Has anybody here been through this, or know an optimal solution to this situation?
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have run a community model where the Y matrix represents counts for 201 taxa (aquatic insects) collected across 206 sites.Initially,  I log transformed the counts and assumed the resulting multivariate Y matrix of counts for each taxa to be normal distributed.  For MCMC, I used 4 chains,  a burn-in of 5000, and the retention of 10000 samples to estimate the posterior. These specifications resulted in a majority of Rhat values being < 1.001 for modeled parameters, and a majority of ESS values were > 10000. So overall, good convergence.

However, being that this data is count data, I wanted to try rerunning the model and assume the multivariate count data was a consequence of a Lognormal Poisson process. For any ecological community count data, this distribution generally makes more sense given the underlying ecological processes at work. However, I was also concerned that, given the size of the matrix (201 taxa X 206 species), convergence might be very difficult to achieve if taxa counts were assumed to not be normally distributed. This logic proved to be true: I reran the model assuming a Lognormal Poisson distribution for the counts using the same MCMC specifications and a histogram indicated that estimated Rhat values ranged from 1 to 2.5 for most estimated parameters (eek!). I reran the model again; however, this time I used a burn-in of 10,000 and retained 30,000 samples to estimate the posterior for each of the 4 chains. Once again, Rhat values were awful. I could rerun the model, and increase the thinning rate, but is there a certain "cutoff" point where it makes more sense to go with the results for the previous model (i.e., where the counts were assumed to be normally distributed)? I realize this is obviously not ideal...

Sincerely,

Josh
